title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
In Part 1, we explored how learning works and applied it to West Nile surveillance. In this session, we use the heart-disease data from Wright et al. and follow the order of their published examples. Open machine-learning-in-epidemiology-with-r.Rproj from the repository root in RStudio. This single project contains both parts. In a fresh project session, run the following in the Console before using the Part 2 scripts:


Code
setwd("part2")


The scripts use part2/ as their working directory. Quarto runs this notebook from its own folder when rendering.
This workshop implements the published examples. Implementation details are documented in the replication record. The frozen data and transformation details are in the data guide.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
1. Meet the data
The task is to distinguish existing heart disease from its absence using clinical measurements. This is a classification example, not a future cardiovascular risk score.


Code
# Article section 1 and appendix: heart-statlog, OpenML 53, version 1.
# Run from part2/. All preprocessing choices are listed in data/README.md.
arff <- readLines("data/raw/heart-statlog.arff")
start <- grep("^@data", arff, ignore.case = TRUE)
heart <- read.csv(text = paste(arff[(start + 1):length(arff)], collapse = "\n"),
                  header = FALSE, strip.white = TRUE)
names(heart) <- c("age", "sex", "chest_pain", "resting_blood_pressure",
  "serum_cholesterol", "fasting_blood_sugar", "resting_ecg", "max_heart_rate",
  "exercise_induced_angina", "ST_depression", "ST_slope", "num_major_vessels",
  "thal", "heart_disease")
stopifnot(nrow(heart) == 270L, ncol(heart) == 14L, !anyNA(heart))
heart$sex <- factor(heart$sex, c(0, 1), c("female", "male"))
heart$chest_pain <- factor(heart$chest_pain, 1:4,
  c("typical angina", "atypical angina", "non-anginal pain", "asymptomatic"))
heart$fasting_blood_sugar <- factor(heart$fasting_blood_sugar, c(0, 1), c("false", "true"))
heart$resting_ecg <- factor(heart$resting_ecg, 0:2,
  c("normal", "ST-T wave abnormality", "left ventricular hypertrophy"))
heart$exercise_induced_angina <- factor(heart$exercise_induced_angina, c(0, 1), c("no", "yes"))
heart$ST_slope <- factor(heart$ST_slope, 1:3, c("upsloping", "flat", "downsloping"))
heart$thal <- factor(heart$thal, c(3, 6, 7), c("normal", "fixed defect", "reversible defect"))
heart$heart_disease <- factor(heart$heart_disease, c("absent", "present"))
numeric_columns <- c("age", "resting_blood_pressure", "serum_cholesterol",
                     "max_heart_rate", "ST_depression", "num_major_vessels")
heart[numeric_columns] <- lapply(heart[numeric_columns], as.numeric)
stopifnot(!anyNA(heart), identical(as.integer(table(heart$heart_disease)), c(150L, 120L)))
dir.create("outputs", showWarnings = FALSE)
dir.create("figures", showWarnings = FALSE)
write.csv(heart, "data/processed/heart.csv", row.names = FALSE)

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 2. Fit and prune a tree — article section 2.1.3
text:
2. Fit and prune a tree — article section 2.1.3
The core script follows the tree examples, then continues through evaluation and resampling. Read it section by section in RStudio. The first trees use the complete dataset for illustration, as in the article; their fitted accuracy would not estimate performance on new patients.


Code
# Article sections 2.1, 3.1 and 3.2. Local seeds make this run reproducible.
source("R/01-data.R")
library(mlr3)
library(mlr3learners)
library(mlr3viz)
set.seed(20261023)
# These first trees illustrate fitting and pruning on all observations,
# as in the article; they do not estimate generalisation performance.
cart <- rpart::rpart(heart_disease ~ ., data = heart)
png("figures/01-tree.png", width = 1500, height = 1000, res = 150)
rpart.plot::rpart.plot(cart)
invisible(dev.off())
deep_cart <- rpart::rpart(heart_disease ~ ., data = heart,
                         control = rpart::rpart.control(minsplit = 2))
png("figures/02-complexity.png", width = 1200, height = 900, res = 150)
rpart::plotcp(deep_cart)
invisible(dev.off())
pruned_cart <- rpart::prune(deep_cart, cp = 0.031)
png("figures/03-pruned-tree.png", width = 1500, height = 1000, res = 150)
rpart.plot::rpart.plot(pruned_cart)
invisible(dev.off())





Default classification tree fitted to the complete heart-disease dataset.


Compare the default tree with the deep tree. The complexity plot connects pruning to the balance between fitting the observed sample and generalising beyond it. The article uses cp = 0.031; we retain that value for the replication.



Cross-validated relative error across candidate complexity parameter values.





Classification tree pruned using cp = 0.031.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 3. Train a neural network — article section 2.2.3
text:
3. Train a neural network — article section 2.2.3
The network script retains the published 64/32-unit architecture, dropout of 0.4, sigmoid output, Adam learning rate of 0.002, binary cross-entropy, 50 epochs, batches of 32, 20% validation and early stopping with patience 10. The data guide explains how we construct 22 inputs.
Run this after configuring Keras. It is separate from the default render because it needs a Python backend.


Code
# Article section 2.2.3, using the current keras3 interface.
source("R/01-data.R")
library(mlr3)
library(keras3)
set_random_seed(20261023)
heart_task <- as_task_classif(heart, target = "heart_disease", positive = "present", id = "heart")
set.seed(20261023)
split <- partition(heart_task, ratio = 2/3)
# Binary predictors use 0/1; remaining nominal predictors use all indicators.
# This explicit reconstruction yields the article's 22 input columns.
x_data <- heart[, setdiff(names(heart), "heart_disease")]
for (nm in c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina")) {
  x_data[[nm]] <- as.integer(x_data[[nm]]) - 1L
}
nominal <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.factor, logical(1))]
contrasts_full <- lapply(x_data[nominal], function(x) contrasts(x, contrasts = FALSE))
x <- model.matrix(~ . - 1, data = x_data, contrasts.arg = contrasts_full)
stopifnot(ncol(x) == 22L, all(is.finite(x)))
# Added for numerical stability: fit numeric scaling on inner training rows only.
# Keras takes the final 20% of supplied training rows for validation.
inner_n <- floor(length(split$train) * 0.8)
fit_rows <- split$train[seq_len(inner_n)]
continuous <- names(x_data)[vapply(x_data, is.numeric, logical(1))]
continuous <- setdiff(continuous, c("sex", "fasting_blood_sugar", "exercise_induced_angina"))
centre <- colMeans(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE])
spread <- apply(x[fit_rows, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, sd)
stopifnot(all(spread > 0))
x[, continuous] <- sweep(sweep(x[, continuous, drop = FALSE], 2, centre), 2, spread, "/")
y <- as.integer(heart$heart_disease == "present")
network <- keras_model_sequential(input_shape = c(22)) |>
  layer_dense(units = 64, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 32, activation = "relu") |>
  layer_dropout(rate = 0.4) |>
  layer_dense(units = 1, activation = "sigmoid")
compile(network, optimizer = optimizer_adam(learning_rate = 0.002),
        loss = "binary_crossentropy", metrics = "accuracy")
training <- fit(network, x[split$train, ], y[split$train], epochs = 50,
  batch_size = 32, validation_split = 0.2, verbose = 0,
  callbacks = list(callback_early_stopping(patience = 10, restore_best_weights = TRUE)))
prob <- as.numeric(predict(network, x[split$test, ], verbose = 0))
class <- ifelse(prob >= 0.5, "present", "absent")
accuracy <- mean(class == as.character(heart$heart_disease[split$test]))
print(accuracy)
write.csv(data.frame(row_id = split$test, truth = heart$heart_disease[split$test],
  probability_present = prob, prediction = class), "outputs/neural-predictions.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(accuracy = accuracy), "outputs/neural-accuracy.csv", row.names = FALSE)
curves <- data.frame(epoch = seq_along(training$metrics$loss),
  loss = training$metrics$loss, val_loss = training$metrics$val_loss)
write.csv(curves, "outputs/neural-loss.csv", row.names = FALSE)
png("figures/05-neural-loss.png", width = 1200, height = 900, res = 150)
matplot(curves$epoch, curves[, c("loss", "val_loss")], type = "l", lty = 1,
        col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), xlab = "Epoch", ylab = "Binary cross-entropy")
legend("topright", c("Training", "Validation"), col = c("steelblue", "firebrick"), lty = 1)
dev.off()
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = "outputs/session-info-neural.txt")


The script saves training and validation loss and the observed test accuracy. The paper’s reported accuracy is not substituted for a local result. When a saved network run is available, its results appear below; these files come from the separate network script, rather than the core notebook render.


   accuracy
1 0.8555556





Training and validation binary cross-entropy across 27 training epochs.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
4. Evaluate predictions — article section 3.1
We now train a probability-producing random forest on two-thirds of the observations and evaluate it on the remaining third. These are the results of our seeded run.


Code
# The article alternates task and heart_task; use one name consistently.
heart_task <- as_task_classif(heart, target = "heart_disease", positive = "present", id = "heart")
set.seed(20261023)
split <- partition(heart_task, ratio = 2/3)
write.csv(data.frame(row_id = c(split$train, split$test),
  subset = rep(c("train", "test"), c(length(split$train), length(split$test)))), "outputs/split.csv", row.names = FALSE)
forest <- lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob", num.threads = 1)
forest$train(heart_task, row_ids = split$train)
forest_pred <- forest$predict(heart_task, row_ids = split$test)
measures <- msrs(c("classif.tpr", "classif.tnr", "classif.ppv", "classif.npv", "classif.acc"))
print(forest_pred$confusion)


         truth
response  present absent
  present      30      8
  absent        7     45


Code
print(forest_pred$score(measures))


classif.tpr classif.tnr classif.ppv classif.npv classif.acc 
  0.8108108   0.8490566   0.7894737   0.8653846   0.8333333 


Code
write.csv(as.data.frame(forest_pred$confusion), "outputs/confusion.csv", row.names = FALSE)
write.csv(data.frame(measure = names(forest_pred$score(measures)),
  value = unname(forest_pred$score(measures))), "outputs/holdout-measures.csv", row.names = FALSE)
for (kind in c("roc", "threshold", "prc")) {
  ggplot2::ggsave(paste0("figures/04-", kind, ".png"),
    ggplot2::autoplot(forest_pred, type = kind), width = 7, height = 5)
}





ROC curve for the random-forest holdout predictions.





Classification error across probability thresholds on the holdout set.





Precision-recall curve for the random-forest holdout predictions.


Discuss sensitivity, specificity, positive and negative predictive value, accuracy and the consequences of choosing a threshold. A good score does not establish causation.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
5. Resample — article section 3.2
The next examples use a 100-tree forest, 3-fold cross-validation, 100 repeated subsamples and 40 bootstrap repetitions. The core script retains those counts.


Code
# Section 3.2 uses a 100-tree forest, rather than the learner default above.
forest100 <- lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob", num.trees = 100, num.threads = 1)
set.seed(20261024)
forest100$train(heart_task, row_ids = split$train)
auc <- msr("classif.auc")
auc_by_subset <- data.frame(subset = c("train", "test"), auc = c(
  forest100$predict(heart_task, row_ids = split$train)$score(auc),
  forest100$predict(heart_task, row_ids = split$test)$score(auc)))
print(auc_by_subset)


  subset       auc
1  train 0.9954043
2   test 0.8980112


Code
write.csv(auc_by_subset, "outputs/train-test-auc.csv", row.names = FALSE)
set.seed(20261025)
cv3 <- resample(heart_task, forest100, rsmp("cv", folds = 3))
write.csv(cv3$score(auc)[, c("iteration", "classif.auc"), with = FALSE],
  "outputs/cv3.csv", row.names = FALSE)
print(cv3$aggregate(auc))


classif.auc 
  0.8994852 


Code
# Same repeat counts as section 3.2; no reduced demonstration budgets.
set.seed(20261026)
subsampling <- resample(heart_task, forest100, rsmp("subsampling", ratio = 2/3, repeats = 100))
set.seed(20261027)
bootstrap <- resample(heart_task, forest100, rsmp("bootstrap", repeats = 40))
resampling_scores <- data.frame(method = c("cv3", "subsampling100", "bootstrap40"),
  auc = c(cv3$aggregate(auc), subsampling$aggregate(auc), bootstrap$aggregate(auc)))
print(resampling_scores)


          method       auc
1            cv3 0.8994852
2 subsampling100 0.9025847
3    bootstrap40 0.9028705


Code
write.csv(resampling_scores, "outputs/resampling-summary.csv", row.names = FALSE)
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = "outputs/session-info-core.txt")


Training and test AUC answer different questions. Resampling estimates how performance changes when the training sample changes.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
section: 6. Tune within the training data — article section 4
text:
6. Tune within the training data — article section 4
The tuning script supplies the missing objects in the published snippets and retains their search ranges and budgets. Run one method at a time from a terminal in this folder:
Rscript R/04-tuning.R grid_search
Rscript R/04-tuning.R random_search
Rscript R/04-tuning.R mbo
Rscript R/04-tuning.R nested
The grid uses resolution 10; random search evaluates 500 configurations; MBO evaluates 30. Nested tuning uses 100 configurations per inner search, 10 inner folds and 10 outer folds. These are substantial runs, so the workshop can inspect the code before running the full searches outside the live session. The test set is excluded from search selection.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
7. Interpret — article section 5
Discuss local explanations, feature effects and feature importance. The article explains these methods but prints no executable interpretation example. We do not introduce a different analysis and label it as replicated article code. Predictive importance describes a fitted model; it does not identify a causal effect.

title: Machine Learning in Epidemiology with R — Part 2
text:
8. Generate synthetic observations — article section 6.2.5
The synthetic-data script follows the adversarial random forest, density estimation and sampling sequence. Its output is labelled synthetic.


Code
# Article section 6.2.5: adversarial random forests.
source("R/01-data.R")
library(arf)
set.seed(20261023)
generator <- adversarial_rf(heart)
density <- forde(generator, heart)
synthetic_heart <- forge(density, n_synth = nrow(heart))
stopifnot(nrow(synthetic_heart) == nrow(heart))
write.csv(synthetic_heart, "outputs/synthetic-heart.csv", row.names = FALSE)
capture.output(sessionInfo(), file = "outputs/session-info-synthetic.txt")


Synthetic rows are generated examples, not additional observed patients.

text:
The original data file uses ARFF (Attribute–Relation File Format), a text format that describes column names and types, followed by one patient per row. “Raw” means the downloaded file before workshop preparation. Its checksum (a fingerprint of the file contents) matches the saved OpenML metadata, confirming that the file has not changed.
270 complete rows; 13 predictors; target counts 150 absent and 120 present.
Train/test split: 180/90 disjoint rows covering all patients.
Default/deep/pruned trees, confusion matrix, five classification measures and three evaluation plots.
Three-fold CV, 100 subsampling repetitions and 40 bootstrap repetitions at the article’s settings.
Neural network with 22 inputs and the article’s architecture/training settings: early stopping after 27 epochs; test accuracy 0.8556. TensorFlow 2.21.0, Python Keras 3.12.4, R keras3 1.5.1.
Bayesian tuning: all 30 configurations, ten-fold inner CV; held-out accuracy 0.7889.
Random search: all 500 configurations, ten-fold inner CV; held-out accuracy 0.8111.
Grid and nested-CV execution paths: reduced smoke runs (grid resolution 2, two folds; nested two evaluations and two inner/outer folds).
ARF/FORDE/FORGE: 270 synthetic observations, saved separately from real data.
R scripts parse, notebook executes and renders with its results and figures.

These are locally observed results, not replacements for the article’s reported results. The notebook reruns the core workflow; saved network and tuning outputs come from separate runs. Package versions for the completed full runs are in the accompanying session-info files.

text:
Environment notes
The installed mlr3learners/XGBoost combination completed the runs but emitted XGBoost deprecation warnings about legacy parameter passing. MBO invoked its built-in random-forest surrogate fallback during this run. ARF ran sequentially without a registered parallel backend.

title: Part 2 — Heart-disease data
text:
Source: OpenML heart-statlog, ID 53, version 1. Downloaded 12 October 2026 from the URL in the saved OpenML metadata. The metadata lists the licence as Public. The original data are attributed to Janosi, Steinbrunn, Pfisterer and Detrano (1988), as cited by the article.
The snapshot has 270 patients, 13 predictors and a binary target: 150 absent, 120 present. It is the OpenML Statlog heart dataset matching the article’s sample size, predictor definitions and outcome.
raw/heart-statlog.arff is unchanged. SHA-256: e16082cc6158f29be2e7b081953cd6edf342760d135bccdb64e191d0834d6300. raw/openml-53-metadata.json preserves the source metadata. processed/heart.csv is regenerated by R/01-data.R.
ARFF (Attribute–Relation File Format) is a text format with a section describing column names and types, followed by the data, with one patient per row. The raw file is the original download before workshop preparation. The preparation script reads it, assigns readable column names and categories, and saves the prepared data as processed/heart.csv.

title: Part 2 — Heart-disease data
text:
Preprocessing
The ARFF target already uses absent/present. The preparation script renames predictors to the article’s appendix names and applies its category definitions. No rows are removed and no imputation is needed. The seven categorical fields are sex, chest_pain, fasting_blood_sugar, resting_ecg, exercise_induced_angina, ST_slope and thal. The other six are explicitly numeric, including the vessel count, as in the appendix.
For the neural network, the three binary predictors use 0/1 and the four other categorical predictors use full indicator encoding, giving 22 columns. Full indicator encoding of all seven categorical predictors would give 25 columns. The article states 22 inputs but does not publish the encoding implementation. Our 22-column construction is therefore an explicit reconstruction. Numeric scaling is fitted on the inner training portion, excluding validation and test rows; scaling details are not specified in the published example. For XGBoost, fixed categorical contrasts produce a numeric design matrix.
The outcome describes heart disease in this teaching sample. It is not a population cardiovascular risk score or a future-event endpoint.

title: About
text:
Federica Gazzelloni is an actuary, statistician, data scientist, author and instructor whose work spans health metrics, actuarial modelling, R and Python, data visualisation and reproducible research. She leads R-Ladies Rome and the Rome R Users Group, and she brings that practical, collaborative style to the workshop materials in this repository.
This experience connects directly to the workshop’s practical approach to machine learning in epidemiology: we start with a clear understanding of the modelling problem, keep the code and data workflow reproducible, and explain how model choices relate to the epidemiological question being asked.

title: About
text:
The two-part learning journey
This workshop is designed as a guided progression through two connected learning experiences:

Part 1 — 28 September 2026: foundations of machine learning, the idea of learning itself, gradient descent, and a West Nile virus prediction workflow.
Part 2 — 23 October 2026: a heart-disease workflow inspired by Wright et al., including trees, neural networks, evaluation, resampling and tuning.

The materials are organised so that participants can move from conceptual understanding to code-based practice without losing sight of the data, the modelling assumptions and the interpretation of results.

Notes

Open machine-learning-in-epidemiology-with-r.Rproj in RStudio. This single project contains both parts.
From a fresh project session, run setwd("part1") or setwd("part2") before running that part’s scripts; their paths are relative to the session folder.

Part 1 preserves the 28 September 2026 teaching materials; Part 2 retains the article workflow and validation notes for locally observed results.

title: Part 1 — Data guide
text:
raw/cdc_nndss_wnv_weekly_2022_2026.csv is a filtered snapshot of the CDC NNDSS Weekly Data table (x9gk-5huc), downloaded on 27 September 2026.
Filter:
label = "Arboviral diseases, West Nile virus disease"
The snapshot contains 17,220 data rows covering 2022 through MMWR week 37 of 2026. It includes states, territories, census regions and totals. advanced/R/01-data.R retains the 50 states, District of Columbia and New York City, then combines New York State and New York City.
The CDC metadata does not provide a licence identifier. The dataset is publicly readable and attributed to the CDC Office of Public Health Data, Surveillance, and Technology. Preserve that attribution and review CDC reuse policies before redistributing the raw file outside this teaching repository.

title: Part 1 — Data guide
text:
Flag handling

Numeric m1: reported current-week cases.
m1_flag = "-": no reported cases, converted to zero.
m1_flag = "U": unavailable, retained as missing.
Other non-numeric flags are also retained as missing.

Do not convert unavailable reporting to zero.

title: Part 2 — Session guide
text:
Friday, 23 October 2026. We use the 270-patient heart-disease dataset matching Wright et al. (2026), with 13 predictors and an absent/present outcome.
Render the core notebook with quarto render. Neural-network, full tuning and synthetic-data scripts are separate runs. Full tuning retains the article budgets and can take much longer than the two-hour session.

title: Part 2 — Session guide
text:
Keras setup
Install the R dependencies, then configure a supported Python backend using keras3::install_keras() in a fresh R session. Alternatively, select an existing compatible Python environment before loading Keras. See the official Keras for R setup guide. Backend installation is a separate step from installing the R package.
The core workflow, neural network, full random/MBO searches and synthetic-data example have been run. See validation results for the results and remaining full-budget checks.

title: Part 2 — Session guide
text:
Scope and provenance
These scripts implement the published examples. The data guide and replication record document data preparation, implementation choices and completed checks. The article’s printed scores are not guaranteed for a different split or environment.

title: Part 2 — Source and replication record
text:
Wright et al. (2026), Machine Learning in Epidemiology, arXiv v1.
OpenML dataset 53, version 1; saved metadata and raw data are in data/raw/.
This workshop implements the article’s published workflow with teaching scripts and explanatory notes. Models and settings follow the published examples.

title: Part 2 — Source and replication record
text:
Workshop implementation
The scripts define data preparation, train/test objects and tuning code, use heart_task consistently and set explicit seeds. Keras uses keras3 instead of the article’s older keras interface, retaining the architecture and training settings. Data encoding/scaling choices are recorded in the data guide. Random-forest threading is fixed to one for reproducibility. The initial forest uses the learner default; the resampling examples use 100 trees, as printed. Tuning is restricted to the training task; nested CV uses an outer and inner 10-fold design. The article’s full grid has up to 10,000 configurations and is not run during a normal notebook render.
The article reports a 100% neural-network test accuracy. That is a reported result for its run, not an expected or guaranteed workshop result. Our outputs are saved separately. Results depend on the random seed, data split, preprocessing and software versions.

title: How a Model Learns in Epidemiology
text:
Slide presentation
Open the 12-slide presentation Download the editable PowerPoint
The slide deck introduces the broader multi-model workflow. The model-performance and variable-importance values shown in the deck are illustrative. The executable notebook below contains the observed results.
By the end, we should be able to answer four questions:

What is the model?
What is the loss?
What is the optimisation procedure?
What is learned?

The central message is:

Learning means using data to determine a model’s parameters or structure. Optimisation is the procedure used to find useful values or structures according to an objective.
